issues.legal_issue: An illegitimate son among the regenerate classes is entitled to maintenance as a right rather than merely to a compassionate allowance.
material_facts: The claimants were found to be the illegitimate sons of their father.
The claimants were excluded from inheritance among the regenerate classes.
issues.conclusion: The claimants were entitled to maintenance for life in recognition of their status as members of their father's family and their exclusion from inheritance; their entitlement was not limited to a compassionate allowance.
issues.legal_principle: Under Mitakshara law, an illegitimate son is entitled to maintenance as long as he lives, in recognition of his status as a member of his father's family and because he is excluded from inheritance among the regenerate classes. The Court relied on Ananthaya v. Vishnu, 17 Mad 160, and considered the description of maintenance as a compassionate rate in Gopalasami Chetti v. Arunachellam Chetti, 27 Mad 32, inappropriate.

rule.if: maintenance_suit and illegitimate_son and regenerate_class_member and excluded_from_inheritance

predicates.maintenance_suit: A claimant sought maintenance from a family member or the family estate.
predicates.illegitimate_son: The claimant was the illegitimate son of the person from whom maintenance was claimed.
predicates.regenerate_class_member: The claimant and father belonged to a regenerate class.
predicates.excluded_from_inheritance: The claimant was excluded from inheritance in that class.

issues.definition: When a maintenance claim is brought by an illegitimate son of a regenerate class who is excluded from inheritance, the son is entitled to lifetime maintenance.

issues.legal_issue: The amount of maintenance must be assessed principally by reference to the income of the relevant property and the claimants' circumstances, rather than increased solely because the father's death left the successor enjoying the property's income.
material_facts: The father's estate included substantial property and investments, with estimated annual property income of about Rs. 45,000 and outstanding debts and other sums exceeding Rs. 5 lakhs.
The father had suffered losses in business transactions.
The claimants were able-bodied adults with their own earning capacity.
After the trial court's judgment, the father died, and the adopted son became the sole person enjoying the income of the properties.
The High Court increased the maintenance award, taking account of the successor's enjoyment of the entire income after the father's death.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the successor's post-death enjoyment of the entire property income was not a relevant reason to increase maintenance, and that the claimants' business losses and earning capacity had to be considered. It reduced the maintenance award to Rs. 125 per month for each claimant.
issues.legal_principle: The exact amount of maintenance is determined principally by the income from the father's properties. The Court also considered the father's business losses and the adult claimants' earning capacity, and held that the change in who enjoyed the property income after the father's death was not a relevant factor for increasing the award.

rule.if: maintenance_suit and substantial_estate_income and business_losses and adult_claimants_earning_capacity and post_death_income_concentrated_in_successor

predicates.maintenance_suit: Claimants sought maintenance from a family estate.
predicates.substantial_estate_income: The estate generated substantial income from its property and investments.
predicates.business_losses: The person whose estate was relevant had suffered losses in business transactions.
predicates.adult_claimants_earning_capacity: The claimants were able-bodied adults with their own capacity to earn.
predicates.post_death_income_concentrated_in_succes: After the father's death, the successor alone enjoyed income that the father had previously enjoyed during his lifetime.

issues.definition: When a maintenance claim concerns a substantial-income estate, the relevant person suffered business losses, the adult claimants could earn, and the successor alone began enjoying the income after the father's death, the maintenance rate is assessed by the estate income and claimants' circumstances rather than by the successor's sole enjoyment of that income.
